opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, when I first went to Husha, I made the mistake a lot of volunteers make. I walked in with a lesson plan that looked like a textbook: vocabulary lists, sentence patterns, a little quiz at the end. Within about ten minutes I could see the kids' eyes glazing over. They were polite, they copied everything down, but nobody was really *there*.

So I threw most of that out and started from a simple question: what do these kids already love doing? The answer was obvious once I looked. They loved running around, competing with each other, and laughing at the teacher when he got something wrong. So I built the classes around games. We'd do relay races where you had to shout the English word for a picture before you could tag the next teammate. We played a version of "Simon Says" for body parts and actions. We did little skits where they'd act out buying vegetables at a market, and the more ridiculous the bargaining got, the more they remembered.

The other thing I learned was to let myself look silly. If I mispronounced something in the local dialect, or drew a terrible cat on the blackboard, the kids would burst out laughing, and that broke the tension. It sent the message that making mistakes is normal, which matters a lot when you're asking a shy ten-year-old to speak a foreign language out loud in front of classmates.

And I tried to connect English to their actual lives rather than to some abstract world in a textbook. Instead of "This is a London bus," it was "This is my grandmother's chicken," or "I walk to school past the river." When the language was about their own village, their families, their animals, suddenly they had something they wanted to say.

Looking back, I'm not sure how much grammar they retained. But I think the more important thing was that, for a few weeks, English stopped being this scary exam subject and became something associated with fun and curiosity. If even a couple of them kept that feeling, I'd count it as a success.

fable-5.1.text:
When I first got to Husha, I quickly realized that the standard approach — vocabulary lists, grammar drills, reading passages aloud — just wasn't going to work. These kids had school all day already, and the last thing they wanted was another hour of someone standing at a blackboard. So I had to let go of the idea that I was there to "teach English" in the conventional sense, and think instead about what would make them actually want to show up.

The biggest shift was turning everything into games. Simple things, honestly. We'd play a version of "Simon Says" with body parts and actions, so they'd be running around shouting "jump" and "touch your nose" without even noticing they were learning. We did a lot of singing too — not textbook songs, but things with rhythm and movement that they could get silly with. I remember one afternoon we spent almost the whole class on a song about animals, and by the end they were making the animal noises and acting them out, and I thought, okay, they've just learned fifteen words and they think they've been playing.

The other thing I learned was to use their own world as the material. Instead of teaching words about airports and supermarkets that had no connection to their lives, we'd talk about the things around them — the fields, the dogs in the village, what their grandmother cooked. I'd ask them to teach me the local names for things first, and then we'd figure out the English together. That reversal mattered a lot. It made them feel like they were the experts, and I was the one learning, which is actually true in a lot of ways.

And I tried to never let anyone feel embarrassed for getting something wrong. A lot of these kids had been told, implicitly or explicitly, that they weren't good at studying. So I made a point of celebrating attempts, even wrong ones. If a kid shouted out the wrong word with total confidence, I'd laugh with them, not at them, and we'd fix it together. Over a few weeks you could see the quieter ones start to raise their hands. That, to me, was the real success — not how many words they memorized, but that they stopped being afraid of trying.

The main thing was to help them feel comfortable trying—even if they made mistakes—and to give them plenty of encouragement.
